title: What is projection pushdown (column pruning) — reading only the columns needed by the query instead of all columns — and how does the Catalyst Optimizer handle it even if you initially select 100 columns but downstream transformations use only 5?

s1_definition.profdef: Projection pushdown, also called column pruning, is an optimization where the Catalyst Optimizer determines the minimal set of columns a query actually needs and instructs the data source to read only those columns, skipping the rest. In columnar formats like Parquet and ORC, each column is stored separately, so reading five columns instead of a hundred reads roughly five percent of the data. Catalyst computes the needed columns by analyzing the entire query, so even if an early step selects many columns, pruning is based on what survives to the final output and the conditions actually used.
s1_definition.analogy: The transactions ledger at the National Bank of India has a hundred fields per record, but a report only needs the account id, the amount, and the date. Without column pruning, the clerk photocopies every field of every record and you discard ninety-seven columns yourself. With projection pushdown, you tell the clerk "only copy these three fields," and because the ledger is stored field-by-field in separate books, the clerk simply never opens the other ninety-seven books. You read a fraction of the paper.
s1_definition.oneliner: Projection pushdown reads only the columns the query needs, so in columnar storage selecting five of a hundred columns reads about five percent of the data.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Projection pushdown, also called column pruning, is an optimization where the Catalyst Optimizer determines the minimal set of columns a query actually needs and instructs the data source to read only those columns, skipping the rest. In columnar formats like Parquet and ORC, each column is stored separately, so reading five columns instead of a hundred reads roughly five percent of the data. Catalyst computes the needed columns by analyzing the entire query, so even if an early step selects many columns, pruning is based on what survives to the final output and the conditions actually used.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The transactions ledger at the National Bank of India has a hundred fields per record, but a report only needs the account id, the amount, and the date. Without column pruning, the clerk photocopies every field of every record and you discard ninety-seven columns yourself. With projection pushdown, you tell the clerk "only copy these three fields," and because the ledger is stored field-by-field in separate books, the clerk simply never opens the other ninety-seven books. You read a fraction of the paper.

**One line to remember:** Projection pushdown reads only the columns the query needs, so in columnar storage selecting five of a hundred columns reads about five percent of the data.

sections.s2_technical:
Columnar formats store each column in its own contiguous region of the file. This layout is what makes column pruning possible: to read a column you seek to its region and read just that, leaving the other columns untouched on disk. So if a query needs only account id, amount, and date, the Parquet reader reads only those three column chunks per row group and never touches the other ninety-seven. The I/O saved is proportional to the fraction of columns you skip, which for wide tables is enormous.

The clever part is how Catalyst decides the needed set. It does not look only at your final select; it analyzes the whole logical plan. It walks the operators and collects every column referenced anywhere that affects the output: columns in the final projection, columns used in filters, columns used in joins, columns used in group-by or aggregations, and columns used in sort. The union of those is the required set. Everything else is pruned. This is why your question's scenario works: even if you start with a select of a hundred columns, if the downstream transformations and final output only use five, Catalyst prunes down to those five, because the ninety-five unused ones never reach any operator that needs them.

The optimizer applies this during its optimization phase, pushing the pruned column list into the scan node of the physical plan. You can confirm it by calling explain and looking at the ReadSchema on the scan — it lists only the pruned columns, not all of them. This works for Parquet and ORC natively, and for JDBC it becomes a narrower SELECT with only the needed columns rather than SELECT star.

A senior-level nuance is that row-based formats like CSV and JSON cannot truly prune columns, because the columns are interleaved on each line, so the reader must read the whole line and then discard unwanted fields — the same weakness as predicate pushdown. Another nuance is nested columns: modern Spark supports nested column pruning, so selecting one field of a struct can avoid reading the sibling fields, though this depends on the Spark version and the nested schema pruning configuration. Finally, projection pushdown and predicate pushdown work together — predicate pushdown skips rows, projection pushdown skips columns, and combining them on Parquet often reduces a scan to a tiny fraction of the file.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's transactions table has a hundred columns, from customer demographics to device metadata. A daily revenue report needs only account id, amount, and date. Reading all hundred columns wastes most of the I/O. This is exactly what projection pushdown solves — the reader reads only the three needed column regions.

Problem 2 — A developer writes a query that first selects fifty columns into an intermediate DataFrame, then later only uses five of them in the final aggregation. They worry the fifty-column select forces reading fifty columns. This is exactly what Catalyst's whole-plan analysis solves — it sees that only five columns survive to the output and conditions, so it prunes to five regardless of the intermediate select.

The demo models a wide schema, a query that references a subset of columns across filters, joins, and the final projection, and computes the pruned column set and the fraction of bytes read, logging the ReadSchema and the savings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transactions table with 100 columns; a query that outputs account id, amount, and date, filters on amount, joins on account id, and groups by date.

Step 1: Catalyst analyzes the whole plan rather than just the final select. It collects the columns the final projection needs — account id, amount, date.

Step 2: It adds columns used in the filter — amount — and columns used in the join — account id — and columns used in the group-by — date. These overlap with the projection, so the union is just account id, amount, and date.

Step 3: Catalyst pushes this three-column list into the scan node as the ReadSchema. The Parquet reader reads only those three column regions per row group and never touches the other ninety-seven.

Step 4: The demo computes the fraction read, roughly three percent, and logs that ninety-five extra columns are skipped on disk and that even an early fifty-column select would still prune to three because only three survive to any operator.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:35:40 [INFO] ReadSchema (pruned): [accountId, amount, txnDate]  (3 of 100 columns)
2026-10-30 04:35:40 [INFO] Projection pushdown reads ~3% of the data
2026-10-30 04:35:40 [INFO] 95 columns skipped on disk — never read because no operator needs them
2026-10-30 04:35:40 [INFO] Even an early select(50 cols) is pruned: Catalyst keeps only what the output/conditions use.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Projection pushdown, also called column pruning, is the optimization where the Catalyst Optimizer figures out the minimal set of columns the query actually needs and tells the data source to read only those, skipping the rest. It is powerful in columnar formats like Parquet and ORC because each column is stored in its own region of the file, so reading three columns out of a hundred reads roughly three percent of the data and never even seeks to the other regions.

The part interviewers probe is how Catalyst decides the needed set, because people assume an early wide select forces reading everything. Catalyst does not look only at the final select — it analyzes the whole logical plan and takes the union of every column that influences the result: the final projection, columns used in filters, columns used as join keys, and columns in group-by, aggregations, or sorts. Anything outside that union is pruned. So even if you select fifty columns into an intermediate DataFrame but only five of them survive into the output and conditions, Catalyst prunes down to those five, because the other forty-five never reach an operator that needs them.

At the National Bank of India our transactions table had around a hundred columns, and most reports needed only a handful like account id, amount, and date. Because we stored the data in Parquet, projection pushdown meant those reports read a few percent of the bytes instead of the whole table, and combined with predicate pushdown skipping irrelevant rows, a scan collapsed to a tiny fraction of the file. I confirm it by calling explain and reading the ReadSchema on the scan node, which lists only the pruned columns. The one caveat I mention is that row-based formats like CSV and JSON cannot truly prune columns because fields are interleaved per line, which is another reason we store analytical data in columnar formats.
